research_dossier.core_conflict: No known planetary transit or stellar pulsation model accounted for the non-periodic massive dimming events.

hook_candidates.text: In 2011, an intact ship sailed alone with dinner still warm on the table.
Seventy-two seconds of signal changed how astronomers scanned the sky forever.
The radar alarm tripped at midnight, pointing toward an empty patch of ocean.
The deepest vault on Earth held fifty records, but zero visitors were allowed inside.
A three-man crew vanished from an island lighthouse without leaving a single trace.
Deep below the Mediterranean floor lies an intact temple no diver was meant to see.
Astronomers logged the exact frequency, yet forty-nine years later the source remains completely silent.
Over twenty miles of ancient stone sat buried beneath coastal sand for a millennium.

narrative_outline.text: Archive photographic plates show the star also underwent secular fading over a century. Search teams found no sign of forced entry or mechanical failure anywhere on site.

narrative_outline.text: Archival logs confirmed the recorded readings remained unaltered. Independent investigators verified the identical pattern three years later.

beats.text: In 2015, Kepler discovered a star whose light dimmed by twenty-two percent.
When an Earth-sized planet orbits in front of a star, it blocks less than one percent of light.
Even a giant planet like Jupiter produces an orderly, predictable dip every few months.
Astronomer Tabetha Boyajian found KIC 8462852 was plunging irregularly by up to twenty-two percent.
The dips lasted days, weeks, and showed zero recurring schedule, baffling stellar astrophysicists.
Early speculations suggested alien megastructures, but color sensors detected red light passing through easier than blue.
This wavelength filtering confirmed the cosmic culprit is likely an uneven cloud of pulverized comets.
A decade later, observatories still monitor the star whose light dimmed twenty-two percent.
